task_title: Inspections, Airworthiness Directives and Preventive Maintenance
objective: By the end of this lesson you can read an airplane's records and say which inspections, checks and airworthiness directives are due, and you can tell which maintenance you may do yourself and how to sign it off.
why: An airplane that is out of inspection or out of AD compliance is unairworthy no matter how well it flies, and the pilot who flies it is the one in violation. Owner-pilots who stay inside the preventive maintenance list, and write it down, save money without putting their certificate at risk.

prereading.what: Owner responsibility, operation after maintenance, annual and 100-hour inspections, altimeter and transponder tests, and maintenance records.
prereading.label: 14 CFR 91.403 to 91.419

prereading.what: What an airworthiness directive is, its legal effect, alternative methods of compliance and special flight permits.
prereading.label: 14 CFR part 39

prereading.what: Who may do maintenance and preventive maintenance, who may approve return to service, and what the record entries must say.
prereading.label: 14 CFR 43.3 to 43.13

prereading.what: The 31 items of preventive maintenance, word for word.
prereading.label: 14 CFR part 43 appendix A(c)

prereading.what: Inspections, ELT, preventive maintenance and entries, special flight permits and ADs, in plain language.
prereading.label: PHAK 9-8 to 9-13

warmup: Think of the last airplane you flew. Without looking, can you say when its annual expires, when its transponder test is due, and whether it has any recurring ADs? Where in the logbooks would you look?

key_terms.def: Inspection every aircraft needs within the preceding 12 calendar months, done and signed by an A&P with an inspection authorization (IA), the manufacturer, or a rated repair station.
Inspection needed every 100 hours of time in service when the aircraft carries people for hire or is provided by the instructor for paid instruction.
From any day of a month to the last day of the same month the following year.
For maintenance records: from the moment the aircraft leaves the surface until it touches down at the next landing.
A legally enforceable FAA rule that fixes an unsafe condition in an aircraft, engine, propeller or appliance.
A different way to fix an AD's unsafe condition. You may use it only after the FAA office named in the AD approves it.
Simple or minor preservation work and replacement of small standard parts, limited to the items listed in part 43 appendix A(c).
The signed record entry that says work was done right and the aircraft may fly again. A pilot's signature approves only the work the pilot did.
A special airworthiness certificate that lets an aircraft that doesn't meet airworthiness requirements, but is safe for the flight, fly to a place for repair or inspection.
VOR test facility: a ground test signal you use to check your VOR receiver. CDI centered should show 0° FROM or 180° TO.

body.p: The rule puts the job on the owner or operator: they are **primarily responsible for maintaining the aircraft in an airworthy condition, including compliance with part 39** (airworthiness directives) [[60:520|14 CFR 91.403(a)]]. They must have it inspected as subpart E requires and have discrepancies between inspections repaired under part 43 [[60:520|14 CFR 91.405(a)]].

That does not let the pilot off the hook. No person may operate a civil aircraft unless it is airworthy, and the pilot in command decides whether it is in condition for safe flight [[60:436|14 CFR 91.7]]. On a rental or club airplane you don't keep the records, but you are the one who flies it.

Look at box 6 of the standard airworthiness certificate. It stays in effect only as long as maintenance, preventive maintenance and alterations are done under parts 21, 43 and 91 and the aircraft stays registered in the United States [[1:238|PHAK 9-8]]. Skip a required inspection or an AD and the paper on the wall no longer means "airworthy".

callout.text: PHAK's owner/operator list: keep a current airworthiness certificate and registration in the aircraft, keep it airworthy including all applicable ADs, make sure maintenance is properly recorded, and keep up with current rules [[1:243|PHAK 9-13]].

check.q: You rent a club airplane. Who is primarily responsible for its AD compliance, and what is your part?
check.a: The owner or operator is primarily responsible [[60:520|14 CFR 91.403(a)]]. As pilot in command you still must not fly it unless it is airworthy and in condition for safe flight [[60:436|14 CFR 91.7]].

callout.text: 91.409(a): No person may operate an aircraft unless, within the preceding 12 calendar months, it has had an annual inspection under part 43 and been approved for return to service by a person authorized by 43.7 (or an inspection for issue of an airworthiness certificate) [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409(a)]].

body.p: **12 calendar months** runs from any day of a month to the last day of the same month the next year [[1:238|PHAK 9-8]]. An annual signed March 3, 2026 is good through March 31, 2027. The annual is done by an A&P mechanic who holds an inspection authorization (IA), the manufacturer, or an appropriately rated repair station [[1:238|PHAK 9-8]].

**The 100-hour** is needed when you carry any person (other than a crewmember) for hire, or give flight instruction for hire in an aircraft you provide. Then the aircraft needs an annual or 100-hour inspection within the preceding 100 hours of time in service [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409(b)]]. Time in service runs from leaving the surface to touching down at the next landing [[60:16|14 CFR 1.1]].

head: Annual
100-hour
rows: Every aircraft, unless 91.409(c) excepts it [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409(a)]]
Carrying persons for hire, or instruction for hire in an aircraft the instructor provides [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409(b)]]
Preceding 100 hours time in service [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409(b)]]
A&P with IA, manufacturer, or rated repair station [[1:238|PHAK 9-8]]
A&P (no IA needed), rated repair station, or manufacturer [[1:238|PHAK 9-8]]
A 100-hour counts only if done by someone allowed to do annuals and entered as an annual [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409(a)]]
An annual counts as a 100-hour [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409(b)]]

body.p: **The 10-hour allowance.** The 100-hour limit may be exceeded by not more than 10 hours while en route to a place where the inspection can be done. The extra time counts toward the next 100 hours [[60:522|14 CFR 91.409(b)]]. There is no such allowance for the annual.

callout.text: Watch out: not every instructional flight needs a 100-hour. The rule covers instruction for hire in an aircraft *the instructor provides*. If you hire a CFI to fly with you in your own airplane, 91.409(b) does not apply to that flight [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409(b)]].

body.p: **Out of annual?** The aircraft may be flown to where the annual can be done only on a special flight permit, and all ADs that are due must be done before that flight [[1:238|PHAK 9-8]]. A special flight permit is a special airworthiness certificate for an aircraft that doesn't meet airworthiness requirements but is safe for a specific flight [[1:242|PHAK 9-12]].

**Other programs.** Annual and 100-hour rules don't apply to aircraft with a special flight permit, experimental, light-sport or provisional certificate, or aircraft on a progressive or large/turbine inspection program [[60:522|14 CFR 91.409(c)]]. A progressive program still inspects the whole aircraft within each 12 calendar months [[60:522|14 CFR 91.409(d)]].

**What the entry looks like.** The inspector records the type and extent of the inspection, the date and total time in service, signature, certificate number and kind, and a statement such as "I certify that this aircraft has been inspected in accordance with (type) inspection and was determined to be in airworthy condition." If it fails, the entry says a dated list of discrepancies was given to the owner [[60:134|14 CFR 43.11(a)]].

check.q: The annual was signed off October 2, 2025. What is the last day you may fly without a new annual?
check.a: October 31, 2026. Twelve calendar months run to the last day of the same month the next year [[1:238|PHAK 9-8]] [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409(a)]].

chunks.title: Altimeter, static system and transponder tests

callout.text: 91.411(a): No person may operate an airplane or helicopter **in controlled airspace under IFR** unless, within the preceding 24 calendar months, each static pressure system, each altimeter, and each automatic pressure altitude reporting system has been tested and inspected under part 43 appendices E and F [[60:524|14 CFR 91.411(a)(1)]].

bullets: **After opening the static system.** Any opening and closing of the static system needs a new static test, except use of the system drain and alternate static valves [[60:524|14 CFR 91.411(a)(2)]].

**After encoder work.** Installation or maintenance on the altitude reporting system where data correspondence error could be introduced needs the integrated system tested [[60:524|14 CFR 91.411(a)(3)]].
**Who.** The airplane's manufacturer, an appropriately rated repair station, or an A&P with an airframe rating (static system only) [[60:524|14 CFR 91.411(b)]].
**Altitude limit.** No IFR in controlled airspace above the highest altitude to which the altimeters and encoder were tested [[60:525|14 CFR 91.411(d)]].

body.p: Why the static system matters: the altimeter and VSI use only static pressure from the static port, and the airspeed indicator uses static plus pitot pressure [[1:204|PHAK 8-2]]. A leak anywhere in those blue lines can corrupt all three.

**Transponder.** No one may use an ATC transponder specified in 91.215(a) unless it was tested and inspected under appendix F within the preceding 24 calendar months [[60:525|14 CFR 91.413(a)]]. 91.215(a) is the "all airspace" paragraph for installed transponders [[60:493|14 CFR 91.215(a)]], so the test applies regardless of airspace [[1:239|PHAK 9-9]]. Any installation or maintenance that could introduce data correspondence error needs a new integrated test [[60:525|14 CFR 91.413(b)]]. **Counting 24 calendar months:** part 91 does not define the term. AC 68-1A defines calendar months as ending on the last day of the month, with the example that 24 calendar months from July 15, 2016 run to July 31, 2018 [[36:7|AC 68-1A 2.3]]. Using that definition here is interpretation, but it matches how PHAK counts the annual [[1:238|PHAK 9-8]].

callout.text: Watch out: don't mix up the two 24-month tests. The altimeter/static/encoder test (91.411) is an **IFR in controlled airspace** rule; a VFR-only flight doesn't need it [[60:524|14 CFR 91.411(a)]]. The transponder test (91.413) applies **any time you use the transponder**, VFR included [[1:239|PHAK 9-9]].

check.q: VFR only today. The altimeter/static test is 30 months old; the transponder test is 20 months old. Legal to fly and use the transponder?
check.a: Yes. 91.411 applies only to IFR in controlled airspace [[60:524|14 CFR 91.411(a)]], and the transponder is within its 24 calendar months [[60:525|14 CFR 91.413(a)]]. You may not file IFR until the 91.411 tests are done.

body.p: No one may operate a U.S.-registered civil airplane unless an approved ELT (personal or automatic type, for part 91 flying) is attached and in operable condition [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(a)(2)]].

head: Rule
What it says
rows: Within 12 calendar months after the last one, for installation, battery corrosion, controls and crash sensor, and enough signal from the antenna [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(d)]]
Replace (or recharge) when the ELT has been in use more than 1 cumulative hour, or when 50% of the battery's useful life has expired [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(c)]]
New expiration date marked on the outside of the ELT and entered in the maintenance record [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(c)]]
May fly up to 90 days with a record entry (date, make, model, serial, reason) and an "ELT not installed" placard in view of the pilot [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(f)(10)]]
Newly bought airplane to where an ELT will be installed, or inop ELT to a repair place; required crew only [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(e)]]
Among others: training operations entirely within 50 NM of the airport where they began, and aircraft equipped for only one person [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(f)]]

body.p: **Testing.** Test per the manufacturer's instructions, ideally in a screened room. If you must test in the airplane: analog 121.5/243 MHz units only in the first 5 minutes after the hour, no more than three audible sweeps. 406 MHz units only per the manufacturer. Airborne tests are not authorized [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]]. Listen on 121.5 before engine shutdown to catch an accidental activation [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]].

callout.text: Changed: since February 1, 2009 the satellites no longer monitor 121.5 or 243.0 MHz. A 121.5-only ELT depends on a nearby ATC facility or an overflying aircraft hearing it [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4]] [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]]. 406 MHz ELTs must be registered with NOAA [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4]].

check.q: Your ELT ran 25 minutes in a test last spring and 40 minutes after a hard landing today. What now?
check.a: Total use is 65 minutes, more than 1 cumulative hour, so the battery must be replaced or recharged, with the new date marked on the unit and in the records [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(c)]].

callout.text: 91.171(a): No IFR using the VOR system unless the VOR equipment is maintained and checked under an approved procedure, or has been operationally checked within the preceding 30 days and found within the limits [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(a)]].

head: Check
Where
Max error
rows: VOT or repair station test signal
At the airport of intended departure
On the surface of the departure airport
Only if no test signal or ground checkpoint is available
Airway radial over a ground point
Prominent point on the airway centerline, preferably more than 20 NM out, at a reasonably low altitude
Both tuned to the same VOR; may replace the checks above

body.p: **Using a VOT.** Tune the VOT frequency. With the CDI centered, the OBS should read 0° with FROM, or 180° with TO. An RMI shows 180° on any OBS setting [[33:70|AIM 1-1-4]]. Airborne use of a VOT is allowed only where the Chart Supplement authorizes it [[33:70|AIM 1-1-4]].

**Ground checkpoints** are a painted circle with an arrow aimed toward the VOR, plus a yellow sign with the station, the check course and DME when applicable [[33:156|AIM 2-3-6]] [[33:157|AIM 2-3-6]]. The circle has a black interior, a yellow ring and a white outer ring, and is never on a runway [[20:107|AC 150/5340-1M 5-3]] [[20:106|AC 150/5340-1M 5-2]] [[33:160|AIM FIG 2-3-20]]. Checkpoint and VOT locations are in the Chart Supplement [[33:71|AIM 1-1-4]].

callout.text: Log every check with **D-E-P-S**: Date, Error (bearing error), Place, Signature, in the aircraft log or other record [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(d)]]. A repair station test signal also needs the station's entry of the bearing it sent and the date [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(d)]].

Older terms: IFH 9-16 says checkpoints are in the "A/FD" and mentions "an appropriate endorsement." The A/FD is now the Chart Supplement U.S. [[1:29|PHAK 1-14]] [[33:71|AIM 1-1-4]]. The rule asks for a log entry with date, place, bearing error and signature, and says nothing about an endorsement [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(d)]].

check.q: Dual VOR check: VOR 1 reads 091° and VOR 2 reads 096° to the same station. Good for IFR?
check.a: No. The two may differ by no more than 4°; 5° is out [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(c)]]. Don't use the VOR for IFR until it is fixed and checks within limits [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(a)(2)]].

body.p: **What they are.** ADs are legally enforceable rules for aircraft, engines, propellers and appliances [[60:125|14 CFR 39.3]]. The FAA issues one when an unsafe condition exists and is likely to exist or develop in other products of the same type design [[60:125|14 CFR 39.5]]. An AD tells you the inspections, conditions and limits, and actions required [[60:125|14 CFR 39.11]].

bullets: Operating a product that doesn't meet an applicable AD is a violation [[60:125|14 CFR 39.7]], and you commit it **each time** you operate [[60:125|14 CFR 39.9]].
An AD still applies even if the product was modified or repaired in the area it covers [[60:125|14 CFR 39.15]].
Two kinds: emergency ADs requiring compliance before further flight, and less urgent ones with a compliance period [[1:242|PHAK 9-12]].
Recurring ADs (for example, inspect every 50 hours) must be done and recorded at every interval [[1:242|PHAK 9-12]].
If an AD conflicts with the service bulletin it is based on, follow the AD [[60:126|14 CFR 39.27]].

callout.text: Common mistake: "the 10-hour allowance covers ADs too." It doesn't. There is no provision to overfly an AD's hour limit unless the AD itself says so [[1:242|PHAK 9-12]]. The 10 hours in 91.409(b) are for the 100-hour inspection only [[60:522|14 CFR 91.409(b)]].

body.p: **Other ways and ferry flights.** Anyone may propose an alternative method of compliance (AMOC) or a change in compliance time, but you may use it only if the manager of the office named in the AD approves it [[60:126|14 CFR 39.19]]. To fly to a shop to do AD work, the FAA may issue a special flight permit unless the AD says otherwise [[60:126|14 CFR 39.23]].

**How compliance is recorded.** The owner keeps a record of the current status of applicable ADs: for each one the method of compliance, the AD number and revision date, and for recurring ADs the time and date the next action is due [[60:526|14 CFR 91.417(a)(2)(v)]]. That status record stays with the aircraft and transfers when it is sold [[60:526|14 CFR 91.417(b)(2)]]. The work itself gets a normal 43.9 entry signed by the person approving it [[60:132|14 CFR 43.9(a)]]. Many owners keep a chronological AD list in the back of each logbook [[1:242|PHAK 9-12]].

check.q: A recurring AD is due at 1,612.4 hours. The airplane is at 1,608.9 and your trip is 5 hours. Can you go and do the AD at the destination?
check.a: No. Only 3.5 hours remain, and you may not overfly an AD limit unless the AD allows it [[1:242|PHAK 9-12]]. Each flight past it is a violation [[60:125|14 CFR 39.9]].

callout.text: 43.3(g): Except for sport pilots, the holder of a pilot certificate issued under part 61 may perform preventive maintenance on any aircraft owned or operated by that pilot which is not used under part 121, 129 or 135. A sport pilot may do it only on an aircraft they own or operate with a light-sport category special airworthiness certificate [[60:130|14 CFR 43.3(g)]].

body.p: Signing it off is a separate step. A person holding **at least a private pilot certificate** may approve an aircraft for return to service after doing preventive maintenance under 43.3(g) [[60:132|14 CFR 43.7(f)]]. Read the two rules together: a student or recreational pilot may do the work under 43.3(g) but may not sign it off under 43.7(f) (interpretation). PHAK 9-12 simply lists student, sport and recreational pilots as excluded [[1:242|PHAK 9-12]].

Preventive maintenance means simple or minor preservation and replacement of small standard parts, not involving complex assembly [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]]. It is **limited to the listed items**, and only when they don't involve complex assembly operations [[60:142|14 CFR part 43 app. A(c)]]. Common ones:

head: Item
Allowed
The catch
rows: Tires; adding oil or air to shock struts; cleaning and greasing wheel bearings [[60:142|14 CFR part 43 app. A(c)]]
Bulbs, reflectors and lenses of position and landing lights [[60:142|14 CFR part 43 app. A(c)(17)]]
Only bulbs, reflectors and lenses; item (16) adds landing light wiring repairs [[60:142|14 CFR part 43 app. A(c)(16)]]
Wheels and skis; cowlings [[60:142|14 CFR part 43 app. A(c)]]
No weight and balance computation; no prop removal or flight control disconnection
Clean or replace spark plugs and set the gap [[60:142|14 CFR part 43 app. A(c)(20)]]
Hose connections; prefabricated fuel lines [[60:143|14 CFR part 43 app. A(c)]]
Fuel and oil strainers or filter elements; batteries [[60:143|14 CFR part 43 app. A(c)]]
Panel-mounted nav/com units with tray-mounted connectors [[60:143|14 CFR part 43 app. A(c)(31)]]
Not autopilots, transponders or DME; operational check before use

body.p: Do the work the manufacturer's way: use the methods in the current maintenance manual or Instructions for Continued Airworthiness, and the tools they call for [[60:135|14 CFR 43.13(a)]]. The result must be at least equal to the original condition [[60:135|14 CFR 43.13(b)]].

callout.text: Older handbook line: PHAK 9-11, quoting part 43, still lists updating panel-mounted navigation databases as preventive maintenance [[1:241|PHAK 9-11]]. The current appendix A(c) list stops at item (31) and does not include it [[60:143|14 CFR part 43 app. A(c)]]. Teach the current rule: 43.3(k) says a database update is **not maintenance at all** when it is started from the flight deck, needs no disassembly and no tools, and follows the manufacturer's instructions [[60:131|14 CFR 43.3(k)]].

check.q: A student pilot owns her own airplane. May she change the spark plugs and sign the airplane back into service?
check.a: No. Approving return to service after preventive maintenance takes at least a private pilot certificate [[60:132|14 CFR 43.7(f)]]; the PHAK excludes student pilots [[1:242|PHAK 9-12]].

chunks.title: The record entry and return to service

callout.text: 43.9(a): Each person who performs preventive maintenance shall make an entry in the maintenance record with (1) a description of the work (or reference to acceptable data), (2) the date it was completed, (3) the name of the person who did it, if not the approver, and (4) the signature, certificate number and kind of certificate of the person approving it. The signature is the approval for return to service, **only for the work performed** [[60:132|14 CFR 43.9(a)]].

body.p: The PHAK's sample description is "changed oil (Shell Aero-50) at 2,345 hours", followed by the date and the pilot's name, signature, certificate number and type of certificate [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]]. A light bulb entry looks the same: what you replaced, the date, then your signature, certificate number and "Private Pilot" (or whatever you hold).

bullets: **No entry, no flight.** No one may operate an aircraft after maintenance or preventive maintenance until it is approved for return to service by a person authorized under 43.7 and the 43.9 entry is made [[60:521|14 CFR 91.407(a)]].

**Flight characteristics.** If the work may have appreciably changed how it flies, no passengers until a pilot with at least a private certificate flies it, checks the work and logs that flight in the aircraft records [[60:521|14 CFR 91.407(b)]]. Not needed if ground tests or inspection show conclusively nothing changed [[60:521|14 CFR 91.407(c)]].
**Keep it.** Maintenance and preventive maintenance records are kept until the work is repeated or superseded, or for 1 year after it is done [[60:526|14 CFR 91.417(b)(1)]].

check.q: You replaced the oil filter element and wrote "replaced oil filter" and the date. You signed it. What is missing?
check.a: Your certificate number and the kind of certificate you hold [[60:132|14 CFR 43.9(a)(4)]]. Until the entry is complete, the airplane isn't approved for return to service [[60:521|14 CFR 91.407(a)]].

chunks.title: Fly it step by step: find what's due in the records

body.p: The owner must keep records of total time in service, life-limited parts, time since overhaul, **current inspection status**, **current AD status**, and the Form 337s for major alterations [[60:526|14 CFR 91.417(a)(2)]]. Work through them in this order:

bullets: 1. **Annual.** Find the last annual entry and its date. It runs out at the end of the same month next year [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409(a)]] [[1:238|PHAK 9-8]].
2. **100-hour,** if the flight is for hire or instruction in an aircraft the instructor provides. Last inspection time + 100, minus any overfly hours used to reach it [[60:522|14 CFR 91.409(b)]].
3. **ADs.** For each recurring AD, read the next-due time and date on the status list [[60:526|14 CFR 91.417(a)(2)(v)]].
4. **ELT.** Inspection within 12 calendar months; battery date on the unit and in the records not passed [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(d)]] [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(c)]].

5. **Transponder** within 24 calendar months for any use [[60:525|14 CFR 91.413(a)]]. **For IFR:** altimeter, static and encoder within 24 calendar months, no static system opened since, and the tested altitude [[60:524|14 CFR 91.411(a)]] [[60:525|14 CFR 91.411(d)]].
6. **For IFR with VOR:** a check entry within the last 30 days [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(a)]].

7. **Open items.** Inoperative items from the last inspection must be on the discrepancy list and placarded [[60:135|14 CFR 43.11(b)]] [[60:521|14 CFR 91.405(d)]]. Also check the airworthiness limitations section for replacement times [[60:520|14 CFR 91.403(c)]].

callout.text: Write the next-due values on one card and keep it with the airplane. The AD status list already requires the next-due time and date for each recurring AD [[60:526|14 CFR 91.417(a)(2)(v)]].

check.q: In the sample table, the student wants to fly a 30-hour block of paid instruction in the school's airplane. What comes due first?
check.a: The recurring AD at 2,505.0 hours (19 hours away), then the 100-hour at 2,512.0 [[60:526|14 CFR 91.417(a)(2)(v)]] [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409(b)]]. And the transponder must be tested before it is used again [[60:525|14 CFR 91.413(a)]].

chunks.title: Risk: going past the list, or not writing it down

body.p: No person may maintain, alter or do preventive maintenance except as part 43 allows [[60:129|14 CFR 43.3(a)]], and part 91 says the same [[60:520|14 CFR 91.403(b)]]. The list is a limit, not a starting point: it covers only the listed work, and only without complex assembly [[60:142|14 CFR part 43 app. A(c)]].
**Jobs that look simple but are not on the list:**

bullets: Replacing a hydraulic hose connection: item (21) excludes hydraulic connections [[60:143|14 CFR part 43 app. A(c)(21)]].
Swapping a tray-mounted transponder, autopilot or DME: item (31) excludes them [[60:143|14 CFR part 43 app. A(c)(31)]].
A cowling that needs the prop off, or wheels that change weight and balance [[60:142|14 CFR part 43 app. A(c)(18)-(19)]].
Overhauling a pressure carburetor or pump: that is a major repair [[60:142|14 CFR part 43 app. A(b)(4)(v)]].

callout.text: Watch out: "I'll just pull the breaker and placard it." The rule says deactivation that involves maintenance must be done and recorded under part 43 [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(3)(ii)]]. FAA guidance in AC 91-67A goes further: deactivating an inoperative system is **not preventive maintenance**, a switch OFF may not remove power, and a person authorized under 43.7 must make the 43.9 entry before flight [[58:24|AC 91-67A 4-2]]. PHAK 9-10 still says deactivation can be as simple as the pilot pulling a breaker [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]], but it points to AC 91-67, which was canceled in 2017 [[58:6|AC 91-67A 1-1]]. Follow the current AC.

body.p: **Not writing it down** is its own violation. Without the entry the aircraft isn't approved for return to service, so no one may fly it [[60:521|14 CFR 91.407(a)]]. Your signature approves only the work you did [[60:132|14 CFR 43.9(a)(4)]], so be exact about what that was.

head: Before you pick up a tool, ask
Why
rows: Is this job on the A(c) list, word for word?
Only listed work counts [[60:142|14 CFR part 43 app. A(c)]]
Does it take apart primary structure or an operating system?
That is complex assembly; get a mechanic [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]]
Do I have the manufacturer's instructions and tools?
Could it change how the airplane flies?
Did I write and sign the entry?

check.q: Your partner wants you to replace a leaking brake line fitting because "it's just a hose." Your answer?
check.a: Not allowed: item (21) covers hose connections except hydraulic connections [[60:143|14 CFR part 43 app. A(c)(21)]]. A mechanic must do and approve it [[60:129|14 CFR 43.3(a)]].

bullets: Counting the annual to the same date next year instead of the end of that month [[1:238|PHAK 9-8]].
Not counting 100-hour overfly time toward the next 100 hours [[60:522|14 CFR 91.409(b)]].
Thinking a 100-hour can replace an annual. Only if done by someone authorized for annuals and entered as an annual [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409(a)]].
Treating the 24-month altimeter test as a VFR rule, or the transponder test as IFR-only [[60:524|14 CFR 91.411(a)]] [[1:239|PHAK 9-9]].
Forgetting the static test after a static line was opened [[60:524|14 CFR 91.411(a)(2)]].
Writing an "endorsement" for a VOR check instead of date, place, bearing error and signature [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(d)]].
Flying past a recurring AD limit to reach the shop without a special flight permit [[1:242|PHAK 9-12]] [[60:126|14 CFR 39.23]].
Doing work that is close to, but not on, the preventive maintenance list [[60:142|14 CFR part 43 app. A(c)]].
Leaving off the certificate number or kind of certificate in the entry [[60:132|14 CFR 43.9(a)(4)]].

check.q: Last 100-hour at 900.0 hours; you used 4 extra hours to reach the shop and it was done at 1,004.0. When is the next one due?
check.a: At 1,100.0 hours. The excess 4 hours count toward the next 100 [[60:522|14 CFR 91.409(b)]].

scenario.title: A Saturday in the hangar before a family IFR trip
scenario.setup: You and a partner co-own a Piper Cherokee. You hold a private pilot certificate with an instrument rating. Today is Tuesday, October 20, 2026, and on Sunday you plan an IFR trip with your family. On Saturday you plan to replace the oil filter element and a missing nonstructural fairing screw. Your partner suggests you also replace a leaking hydraulic brake line fitting and swap in the spare transponder from his old airplane: "It slides into the tray, nobody will know, we'll log it later." The last annual entry is dated October 9, 2025.

questions.q: Which of the four jobs may you do yourself as preventive maintenance?
questions.a: The oil filter element (item 23) and the nonstructural fastener (item 26) [[60:143|14 CFR part 43 app. A(c)]]. The hydraulic fitting is excluded by item (21), and transponders are excluded from item (31) [[60:143|14 CFR part 43 app. A(c)]]. You may do PM as an owner with a part 61 certificate [[60:130|14 CFR 43.3(g)]].

questions.q: After the filter change, what must the entry say before anyone flies?
questions.a: A description of the work, the date completed, and your signature, certificate number and kind of certificate [[60:132|14 CFR 43.9(a)]]. Until then the airplane isn't approved for return to service [[60:521|14 CFR 91.407(a)]].

questions.q: What is wrong with "swap the transponder and log it later"?
questions.a: It isn't preventive maintenance, so you may not do it [[60:129|14 CFR 43.3(a)]] [[60:143|14 CFR part 43 app. A(c)(31)]]. No one may fly after maintenance without the approval and entry [[60:521|14 CFR 91.407(a)]], and a newly installed transponder needs the integrated test before use [[60:525|14 CFR 91.413(b)]].

questions.q: The brake fitting still leaks Saturday night. Can you fly Sunday?
questions.a: Not until a mechanic repairs it and approves it for return to service. The owner must have discrepancies repaired under part 43 [[60:520|14 CFR 91.405(a)]], and you may not fly an unairworthy airplane [[60:436|14 CFR 91.7]].

questions.q: The annual is dated October 9, 2025. Is it good for Sunday, October 25, 2026, and when does it run out?
questions.a: Yes. It is good through October 31, 2026, the last day of the same month a year later [[1:238|PHAK 9-8]] [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409(a)]]. Book the next annual now: there is no grace period.

skills.do: At a flight review or IPC, open the airplane's logbooks and show when the annual (and 100-hour if needed), each recurring AD, the ELT inspection and battery, the transponder test, and for IFR the altimeter/static test and VOR check are next due.
skills.practice: Build a one-page due list from your airplane's records using the 91.417(a)(2) items [[60:526|14 CFR 91.417(a)(2)]]. Have your instructor quiz you on it, then check it against the rules in 91.409, 91.411, 91.413, 91.207 and 91.171 [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409]] [[60:524|14 CFR 91.411]] [[60:525|14 CFR 91.413]] [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(d)]] [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171]].

quiz.q: Who is primarily responsible for keeping an aircraft airworthy, including AD compliance?
options: The mechanic who did the last annual
The owner or operator
The pilot in command only
The FAA inspector who issued the certificate
quiz.why: The owner or operator is primarily responsible, including compliance with part 39 [[60:520|14 CFR 91.403(a)]]. The PIC still decides whether it is in condition for safe flight [[60:436|14 CFR 91.7]].

quiz.q: An annual inspection is signed off January 15, 2026. Without another annual, the last day you may fly is:
options: January 14, 2027
January 15, 2027
January 31, 2027
December 31, 2026
quiz.why: 12 calendar months run from any day of a month to the last day of the same month the next year [[1:238|PHAK 9-8]].

quiz.q: Which flight requires the aircraft to be within a 100-hour inspection?
options: A CFI giving paid lessons in an airplane the CFI provides
An owner flying alone to a fly-in
An owner taking paid instruction from a freelance CFI in the owner's airplane
A ferry flight under a special flight permit
quiz.why: 91.409(b) covers carrying persons for hire and instruction for hire in an aircraft the instructor provides [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409(b)]]. Special flight permits are excepted [[60:522|14 CFR 91.409(c)(1)]].

quiz.q: The 24-month altimeter, static system and encoder test of 91.411 is required to:
options: Fly in any controlled airspace, VFR or IFR
Fly IFR in controlled airspace
Fly IFR, every 12 calendar months
Fly above 18,000 ft only
quiz.why: 91.411(a) applies to operating an airplane or helicopter in controlled airspace under IFR, within the preceding 24 calendar months [[60:524|14 CFR 91.411(a)(1)]]. VFR is not covered.

quiz.q: When must an ELT battery be replaced or recharged?
options: At every annual inspection
Every 24 calendar months
When the ELT fails its 12-month inspection only
After more than 1 cumulative hour of use, or when 50% of its useful life has expired
quiz.why: Both triggers are in 91.207(c), and the new expiration date goes on the unit and in the records [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(c)]].

quiz.q: Using a designated airborne VOR checkpoint, the maximum allowed bearing error is:
quiz.why: Airborne checkpoints allow ±6°; VOT and ground checkpoints allow ±4° [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(b)]].

options: A legally enforceable rule that fixes an unsafe condition in a product
A manufacturer's recommendation that part 91 owners may skip
A rule that applies only to aircraft used for hire
A notice that expires at the next annual
quiz.why: ADs are legally enforceable rules for aircraft, engines, propellers and appliances [[60:125|14 CFR 39.3]], issued for an unsafe condition likely in other products of the same design [[60:125|14 CFR 39.5]].

quiz.q: Which of these is preventive maintenance a private pilot owner may do?
options: Replacing a hydraulic brake hose connection
Swapping a tray-mounted transponder
Replacing safety belts
Overhauling a pressure type carburetor
quiz.why: Replacing safety belts is item (14) [[60:142|14 CFR part 43 app. A(c)(14)]]. Hydraulic connections and transponders are excluded [[60:143|14 CFR part 43 app. A(c)]], and carburetor overhaul is a major repair [[60:142|14 CFR part 43 app. A(b)(4)(v)]].

quiz.q: Your preventive maintenance entry must include:
options: The description, tach time and your IA number
The description, the date, and your signature, certificate number and kind of certificate
The date and an instructor's endorsement
Only your signature; descriptions are optional for preventive maintenance
quiz.why: These are the 43.9(a) items; the signature approves return to service only for that work [[60:132|14 CFR 43.9(a)]].

takeaways: Annual: within the preceding 12 calendar months, good to the end of the month. 100-hour only for hire or for instruction in an aircraft the instructor provides; overfly hours count toward the next one.
Transponder test: 24 calendar months for any use. Altimeter, static and encoder test: 24 calendar months for IFR in controlled airspace, and again after the static system is opened.
ELT: inspect within 12 calendar months; replace the battery after 1 cumulative hour of use or 50% of its life.
VOR for IFR: checked within 30 days. ±4° on the ground, ±6° airborne, 4° between dual VORs. Log date, error, place, signature.
ADs are law. No overflying a limit unless the AD allows it. Record the method, number, revision date and next due.
Preventive maintenance is only the appendix A(c) list, signed by at least a private pilot with description, date, signature, certificate number and kind. No entry, no flight.
cfi_notes: Bring the actual logbooks of the airplane to the flight review and have the pilot build the due list. Reading real entries teaches more than any table.

PHAK 9-9 ties the altimeter test to IFR in controlled airspace, then adds that it "applies to all aircraft being operated in controlled airspace," which can be misread as covering VFR. It also says "24 months." 91.411(a) covers airplanes and helicopters under IFR in controlled airspace, within 24 calendar months. Teach the rule text.

PHAK 9-10 says deactivation may be as simple as the pilot pulling a circuit breaker, and refers to AC 91-67. AC 91-67A (10/16/23) para 1.4 says AC 91-67 was canceled on November 3, 2017, and para 4.2.2 says deactivation is not preventive maintenance and a person authorized under 43.7 must make the 43.9 entry. The rule itself (91.213(d)(3)(ii)) only says deactivation that involves maintenance follows part 43; teach the rule and present the AC as current FAA guidance.

PHAK 9-11 lists updating panel-mounted navigation databases as preventive maintenance. The current appendix A(c) has 31 items and doesn't include it, and 43.3(k) says qualifying database updates are not maintenance. Teach the current rule text.

IFH 9-16 refers to the "A/FD" and an "appropriate endorsement" for VOR checks, and gives 108.0 MHz as the VOT frequency to tune. Current terms: Chart Supplement, a 91.171(d) log entry, and the published VOT frequency; AIM 1-1-4 gives 108.0 MHz as the frequency normally approved for repair station test signals.

PHAK 9-12's AD record list mixes 91.417(a)(1) and (a)(2)(v) and says AD number and revision date "if recurring." 91.417(a)(2)(v) requires the number and revision date for every applicable AD, plus next-due time and date for recurring ones.

PHAK 9-12 says student, sport and recreational pilots may not do preventive maintenance. The CFR splits it: 43.3(g) lets any part 61 pilot except a sport pilot (outside light-sport aircraft) do the work, and 43.7(f) lets only a private pilot or higher approve the return to service. Teach both rules; the practical result for a student pilot is the same. For the 100-hour, walk through the 91.409(b) wording: for hire, and in an aircraft the instructor provides.
PHAK 9-8 frames the annual for aircraft of 12,500 lb or less flown for business or pleasure. 91.409(a) itself has no weight limit; the exceptions are in 91.409(c) and (e).
gaps: Part 65 (mechanic and inspection authorization privileges) is not in the sources, so who may perform annual and 100-hour inspections comes from PHAK 9-8 only.

Appendix A(c) doesn't name an oil change word for word; the PHAK uses one as its sample entry. Item (23) covers oil filter elements. AC 43-12 (Preventive Maintenance) and AC 43-9 (Maintenance Records) are referenced by AC 91-67A but not uploaded.
No source says whether a tach or Hobbs meter should track time in service; only the 14 CFR 1.1 definition is given.
The AIH (8-10) says ADs can be downloaded from www.faa.gov, but no source names the current AD search tool. PHAK 9-12 and 9-13 cite rgl.faa.gov, which may be out of date.

The test procedures in part 43 appendices E and F and the annual scope in appendix D are not taught in detail here.",
  "14 CFR 1.1 and part 91 do not define \"calendar months.\" The lesson counts 12 and 24 calendar months to the last day of the month using PHAK 9-8 (annual) and the AC 68-1A 2.3 definition, which was written for BasicMed. That is interpretation for the ELT, transponder and altimeter tests.

activities.title: True or false: inspections and tests
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: An annual signed April 2 is good until April 2 of the next year.
cards.why: False. It is good through April 30 of the next year: 12 calendar months end on the last day of the month [[1:238|PHAK 9-8]].

cards.s: A 100-hour inspection can count as the annual if a person authorized to do annuals does it and enters it as an annual.
cards.why: True. That is the only way a 100-hour substitutes for an annual [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409(a)]].

cards.s: You hire a freelance CFI for instrument training in your own airplane. The airplane needs a 100-hour inspection.
cards.why: False. 91.409(b) covers instruction for hire in an aircraft the instructor provides [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409(b)]].

cards.s: Hours flown past the 100-hour limit to reach the shop don't count toward the next 100 hours.
cards.why: False. Up to 10 hours are allowed en route, and the excess must be included in the next 100 [[60:522|14 CFR 91.409(b)]].

cards.s: The 24-month altimeter, static and encoder test is required to fly IFR in controlled airspace.
A transponder overdue for its 24-month test may still be used on VFR flights.
cards.why: False. 91.413 applies to using the transponder, regardless of airspace [[60:525|14 CFR 91.413(a)]] [[1:239|PHAK 9-9]].

activities.title: Read the VOR ground checkpoint marking
activities.intro: Drag each name to its numbered pin.

activities.title: How often is it due?
activities.intro: Tap an inspection or check, then its interval.

pairs.r: Each 100 hours in service when flown for hire
24 calendar months, for IFR in controlled airspace
12 calendar months after the last ELT inspection
Preceding 30 days, for IFR using VOR

activities.title: May the owner-pilot do it?
activities.intro: Tap a clue, then tap where it belongs.
buckets: Preventive maintenance: pilot may do it

items.t: Replace a burned-out landing light bulb
Clean the spark plugs and set the gap
Swap a tray-mounted panel nav/com radio
Add air to a landing gear shock strut
Replace a hydraulic brake hose connection
Replace a cowling that requires removing the propeller
Deactivate an inoperative system for a 91.213(d) deferral

activities.title: From wrench to return to service
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the steps in order, then tap Check.
steps: Find the job, word for word, on the part 43 appendix A(c) list
Get the manufacturer's instructions and the tools they call for
Do the work so the part is at least equal to its original condition
Write the entry: description of the work and the date
Sign it with your certificate number and kind of certificate
If flight characteristics may have changed, fly it, check it and log it before carrying passengers

activities.title: Work out what's due
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: The last 100-hour was at 1,200.0 hours. You used 6 extra hours to reach the shop, and the next 100-hour was done at 1,306.0. At what time in service is the following one due?
items.why: The excess hours count toward the next 100: it was due at 1,300.0, so the next is 1,300.0 + 100 = 1,400.0, not 1,406.0 [[60:522|14 CFR 91.409(b)]].

items.q: A recurring AD requires an inspection every 50 hours. It was last done at 2,215.5 hours. The airplane now shows 2,241.0. How many hours may you fly before it is due?
items.why: Next due 2,215.5 + 50 = 2,265.5. 2,265.5 - 2,241.0 = 24.5 hours. No overfly unless the AD allows it [[1:242|PHAK 9-12]].

items.q: The ELT manufacturer gives the battery a useful life of 6 years. How many years after installation must it be replaced under the 50% rule?
items.why: Replace when 50% of the useful life has expired: 6 x 0.5 = 3 years [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(c)(2)]].

items.q: Dual VOR check: VOR 1 shows 093° and VOR 2 shows 098° to the same station. What is the difference in degrees?
items.why: 098 - 093 = 5°. The limit is 4°, so this VOR may not be used for IFR until fixed [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(c)]].

items.q: An annual is signed March 3, 2026. Through what day of March 2027 may you fly on it? (Type the day of the month.)
items.why: 12 calendar months end on the last day of the same month the next year: March 31, 2027 [[1:238|PHAK 9-8]].

activities.title: Can you legally fly tomorrow's IFR trip?
activities.intro: You own N4417R, a Cessna 172 with one VOR and an altitude-reporting transponder. Today is October 20, 2026. Tomorrow you plan an IFR trip with a friend aboard, returning after dark. You open the logbooks.

steps.s: The last annual was signed November 9, 2025. The airplane has flown 140 hours since, with no 100-hour. Your friend isn't paying you. Inspection status?
options: Grounded: it's more than 100 hours since the last inspection
Legal: the annual is good through November 30, 2026, and no 100-hour is needed for this flight
Legal only after a 100-hour, because there is a passenger
Legal for 10 more hours under the overfly allowance
steps.why: The annual runs to the end of November 2026 [[1:238|PHAK 9-8]]. A 100-hour is needed only when carrying persons for hire or giving instruction for hire in an aircraft you provide [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409(b)]].

steps.s: The altimeter, static and encoder test and the transponder test were done in December 2024. But last month a mechanic replaced a cracked static line fitting, and there is no static test entry after that work.
options: Fine: the 24-month tests are good until December 2026
Fine, if you use the alternate static source for the trip
No IFR in controlled airspace until the static system is tested again
Only the transponder needs a new test
steps.why: Opening and closing the static system, other than drains and alternate static valves, requires a new appendix E test before IFR in controlled airspace [[60:524|14 CFR 91.411(a)(2)]].

steps.s: The shop does the static test today and signs it off. Next: the last VOR check entry is 41 days old. The departure airport has a VOT.
options: Have a mechanic endorse your logbook for VOR use
Tune the VOT, center the CDI, look for 0° FROM or 180° TO within ±4°, then log date, place, error and signature
Accept up to ±6°, since it's a ground check
Retune your one VOR to two stations and compare them
steps.why: A VOT check at the departure airport allows ±4° [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(b)(1)]]. CDI centered should show 0° FROM or 180° TO [[33:70|AIM 1-1-4]]. The entry needs date, place, bearing error and signature [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(d)]].

steps.s: On preflight the left position light bulb is burned out. You have an approved spare and the maintenance manual steps.
options: Placard it INOP and fly at night under 91.213(d)
Replace it; a bulb needs no entry
Wait for a mechanic; pilots may not touch lighting
Replace it yourself, then make a 43.9 entry with description, date, signature, certificate number and kind
steps.why: Bulbs of position lights are item (17) [[60:142|14 CFR part 43 app. A(c)(17)]], which you may do as owner [[60:130|14 CFR 43.3(g)]] and must record [[60:132|14 CFR 43.9(a)]]. Position lights are required for night flight [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(c)(2)]].

steps.s: Last page: a recurring AD is next due at 3,312.0 hours. The airplane shows 3,309.5, and the round trip is 4.5 hours.
options: Have the AD done before the trip, or plan to land before 3,312.0
Go: you may overfly by up to 10 hours
Go: ADs don't apply to private part 91 flights
Go, and have it done at the destination with a note in the log
steps.why: There is no provision to overfly an AD limit unless the AD says so [[1:242|PHAK 9-12]], and every flight out of compliance is a violation [[60:125|14 CFR 39.9]].

final_quiz.q: A school airplane is used for paid instruction. Its last 100-hour was at 1,850.0 hours, and it now shows 1,948.0. What does 91.409(b) allow?
options: 2 more hours, then up to 10 more only to fly to a place where the inspection can be done
12 more hours of instruction, using the 10-hour allowance
Unlimited flying until the annual is due
No more flight at all without a special flight permit
final_quiz.why: Due at 1,950.0. The limit may be exceeded by no more than 10 hours, and only while en route to where the inspection can be done [[60:522|14 CFR 91.409(b)]].

final_quiz.q: Your annual ran out yesterday. The nearest IA is at an airport 40 NM away. How do you legally get the airplane there?
options: Fly it there with no passengers; short repositioning flights are allowed
Use the 10-hour allowance
Get a special flight permit, and complete any ADs that are due before the flight
Have an A&P sign a 100-hour and fly on that
final_quiz.why: An airplane overdue for its annual may fly to the inspection site on a special flight permit, with all due ADs done first [[1:238|PHAK 9-8]]. A 100-hour substitutes only if done by someone authorized for annuals and entered as an annual [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409(a)]].

final_quiz.q: Your altimeters and encoder were tested to 12,000 ft. On an IFR flight in controlled airspace, ATC offers 14,000 ft. You should:
options: Accept; the tested altitude matters only in Class A
Decline; you may not fly IFR in controlled airspace above the tested altitude
Accept, as long as the transponder test is current
Accept for no more than 10 minutes
final_quiz.why: No IFR in controlled airspace above the maximum altitude to which all altimeters and the encoder were tested [[60:525|14 CFR 91.411(d)]].

final_quiz.q: In flight you selected the alternate static source to troubleshoot an altimeter. Does the static system need a new test before the next IFR flight?
options: Yes; any opening of the static system needs a test
Yes, but only if the altimeter changed more than 50 ft
Only at the next annual
No; using the alternate static valve is excepted
final_quiz.why: 91.411(a)(2) excepts use of the system drain and alternate static pressure valves [[60:524|14 CFR 91.411(a)(2)]].

final_quiz.q: Your ELT goes to the shop for repair. May you keep flying the airplane?
options: Yes, up to 90 days, with a records entry and an "ELT not installed" placard in view of the pilot
Yes, indefinitely, as long as you stay VFR
No, not until the ELT is reinstalled
Yes, but only on a special flight permit
final_quiz.why: 91.207(f)(10) allows up to 90 days after removal, with the records entry (date, make, model, serial, reason) and the placard [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(f)(10)]].

final_quiz.q: You need to test a 406 MHz ELT installed in your airplane. What does the AIM say?
options: Test it in flight once a year
Test it in the first 5 minutes after the hour, three sweeps maximum
Test it only per the unit manufacturer's instructions, never in flight
No test is needed; the satellites check it automatically
final_quiz.why: 406 MHz ELTs are tested only per the manufacturer's instructions, and airborne tests are not authorized. The 5-minute, three-sweep rule is for analog 121.5/243 MHz units [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]].

final_quiz.q: You check your VOR over a designated airborne checkpoint and see 4° of error. What must you record?
options: Your name and the VOR frequency
A CFII's endorsement
The date and your signature only
The date, place, bearing error and your signature
final_quiz.why: 91.171(d) requires date, place, bearing error and signature in the aircraft log or other record. 4° is within the ±6° airborne limit [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(d)]] [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(b)(3)]].

final_quiz.q: No VOT, ground checkpoint or airborne checkpoint is available. Which in-flight check meets 91.171?
options: Any radial at any distance, within ±4°
An airway radial over a prominent ground point, preferably more than 20 NM from the VOR, within ±6°
Compare the VOR with the GPS course, within ±6°
Fly over the VOR station and note the indication
final_quiz.why: That is the 91.171(b)(4) check, flown at a reasonably low altitude, with a 6° limit [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(b)(4)]] [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(b)(4)]].

final_quiz.q: Your mechanic suggests a cheaper way to meet an AD than the one it prescribes. When may you use it?
options: Right away, if the mechanic signs it off
After the next annual inspection
Only after the manager of the office named in the AD approves it
Never; ADs allow no alternatives
final_quiz.why: Anyone may propose an alternative method of compliance, but you may use it only if the manager approves it [[60:126|14 CFR 39.19]].

final_quiz.q: An AD and the service bulletin it incorporates give different instructions. Which do you follow?
options: The AD
The service bulletin, because it is more detailed
Whichever the POH lists
Whichever is less restrictive
final_quiz.why: If the service document conflicts with the AD, you must follow the AD [[60:126|14 CFR 39.27]].

final_quiz.q: A sport pilot owns a standard-category Cessna 150. May she change its spark plugs and sign it off?
options: Yes; spark plugs are item (20)
Yes, if a CFI supervises
Yes, after a ground run-up
No; sport pilots may do preventive maintenance only on light-sport category aircraft they own or operate
final_quiz.why: 43.3(g) excludes sport pilots except on aircraft with a light-sport category special airworthiness certificate [[60:130|14 CFR 43.3(g)]].

final_quiz.q: You sell your airplane. Which records must transfer with it?
options: Only the last annual entry
Total time, current inspection and AD status, life-limited parts, overhaul times and major alteration forms
Only records less than 1 year old
None; the buyer starts new logbooks
final_quiz.why: The 91.417(a)(2) records are retained and transferred with the aircraft when it is sold [[60:526|14 CFR 91.417(b)(2)]] [[60:527|14 CFR 91.419(a)]]. The other (a)(1) work records go to the buyer too, though the buyer may let the seller keep them [[60:527|14 CFR 91.419(b)]]. So "only the last annual" or "only the last year" is wrong.

final_quiz.q: You update your GPS navigator's database from the cockpit by inserting a data card, following the manufacturer's steps, with no tools and no disassembly. Under current rules this is:
options: Preventive maintenance under appendix A(c)
Maintenance that needs an A&P sign-off
Not maintenance, under 43.3(k)
A minor alteration needing a Form 337
final_quiz.why: Database updates started from the flight deck without disassembly or tools are not considered maintenance and may be done by pilots following the manufacturer's instructions [[60:131|14 CFR 43.3(k)]].

final_quiz.q: You replaced a cowling (no prop removal, no flight control disconnection) and signed the entry. Ground checks show conclusively that flight characteristics are unchanged. Before carrying passengers you need:
options: Nothing more; the signed entry returns it to service
A test flight by a private pilot, logged in the aircraft records
An A&P's inspection of your work
A new annual inspection
final_quiz.why: Item (19) work with a 43.9 entry returns the aircraft to service [[60:142|14 CFR part 43 app. A(c)(19)]] [[60:521|14 CFR 91.407(a)]]. A test flight isn't needed when ground tests show conclusively nothing changed [[60:521|14 CFR 91.407(c)]].
